questions.stem: Economics is best defined as the study of how

options.text: governments raise revenue and spend it
individuals and societies allocate scarce resources among competing wants
traders make the largest possible profit from buying and selling
money is printed and circulated by banks

questions.explanation: The subject matter of economics is the allocation problem created by scarcity: unlimited wants set against limited resources. Every branch of the subject — demand, production, trade, taxation — is an application of that single idea.

distractorRationale.a: This describes public finance, which is only one branch of economics
distractorRationale.c: This describes business or commerce; economics studies whole societies, not only sellers
distractorRationale.d: This describes monetary management, again only one part of the subject

questions.stem: In economics, scarcity means that

options.text: a commodity has completely disappeared from the market
resources are limited relative to the wants they must satisfy
there is not enough money in circulation

questions.explanation: Scarcity is a relationship, not a quantity. However much of a resource exists, it is scarce as long as people want more of it than is available at zero price. This is why scarcity is permanent and universal.

distractorRationale.a: That is a shortage, which is temporary and affects a particular commodity
distractorRationale.c: A high price is a consequence of scarcity, not its definition; cheap goods are scarce too
distractorRationale.d: Scarcity concerns real resources such as land, labour and capital, not the supply of money

questions.stem: A list of unsatisfied wants arranged in order of their relative importance is called
questions.explanation: A scale of preference ranks wants from the most urgent downwards. It is the tool that turns the vague feeling of wanting many things into a decision about what to buy first.

distractorRationale.a: A budget matches planned spending to expected income; it does not by itself rank wants by urgency
distractorRationale.c: Opportunity cost is the alternative sacrificed once the choice has been made
distractorRationale.d: A production possibility schedule shows combinations of two goods an economy can produce, not a ranking of a consumer's wants

questions.stem: Which of the following is a free good?
questions.explanation: A free good is abundant relative to the want it satisfies and needs no resources to obtain, so it carries no price and no opportunity cost. Atmospheric air meets all three tests.

distractorRationale.a: Sachet water uses capital, labour and packaging, so it is an economic good with a price
distractorRationale.b: Firewood looks free but labour and time are used to gather and carry it, which is a real cost
distractorRationale.d: Kerosene must be refined and distributed, so it is scarce and priced

questions.stem: Choice is unavoidable in every economy mainly because

options.text: human wants are unlimited while the resources to satisfy them are limited
government fixes the prices of most goods
there is too little money in circulation

questions.explanation: Scarcity is the cause and choice is the consequence. Because the same resource can be used in several ways but not all at once, some wants must be postponed or abandoned — and that decision is a choice.

distractorRationale.b: Even a modest person with few wants faces choice, because time and income are still limited
distractorRationale.c: Price control creates shortages in particular markets; choice exists whether or not prices are controlled
distractorRationale.d: Printing more money would raise prices, not remove the limit on real resources

questions.stem: Ngozi has ₦8,000 and her scale of preference is: textbook ₦5,000, school bag ₦2,000, calculator ₦1,500, sandals ₦3,000. Working strictly down her scale of preference, how many of these wants can she satisfy? Give a number only.
questions.explanation: Starting at the top: ₦8,000 − ₦5,000 for the textbook leaves ₦3,000; ₦3,000 − ₦2,000 for the bag leaves ₦1,000. The calculator costs ₦1,500, which she can no longer afford, so she stops after two wants.

questions.stem: Every good that satisfies a human want is an economic good.
questions.explanation: False. Free goods such as atmospheric air and sunshine satisfy genuine wants, yet they are abundant, cost nothing to obtain and carry no price. Only scarce goods that require resources are economic goods.

distractorRationale.a: This assumes usefulness alone makes a good economic; scarcity, not usefulness, is the test

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of human wants?

options.text: Wants are competitive because the same resources can satisfy different wants
Once a want has been satisfied it never arises again
Wants vary from one person to another and change over time

questions.explanation: Wants are recurrent: food satisfied today returns tomorrow, and clothing wears out. That recurrence is precisely why production must continue, so option c contradicts a basic feature of wants.

distractorRationale.a: True — satisfying one want reveals the next, so the list never closes
distractorRationale.b: True — the same naira or the same hour of labour cannot serve two wants at once
distractorRationale.d: True — wants differ with age, income, culture and season

questions.stem: What is the primary reason that resources are considered limited in economics?

options.text: Resources are finite and cannot be expanded indefinitely.
Resources are only available in certain regions.
Resources are only useful for a limited time.

questions.explanation: Resources are limited because they are finite in nature. This limitation forces individuals and societies to make choices about how to allocate these scarce resources effectively.

distractorRationale.b: While some resources may be depleted, this is not the primary reason for their limited nature.
distractorRationale.c: Resources can be found in various regions, and their availability is not restricted to specific locations.
distractorRationale.d: Resources can have long-term utility, and this does not define their limited nature.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes 'wants' in economics?

options.text: Wants are the basic necessities of life.
Wants are desires for goods and services that can be satisfied.
Wants are limited to material goods only.
Wants are the same as needs.

questions.explanation: In economics, wants refer to the desires for goods and services that can fulfill human satisfaction. They are not limited to necessities and can vary widely among individuals.

distractorRationale.a: Basic necessities are a subset of wants, but not all wants are necessities.
distractorRationale.c: Wants can include both material and non-material goods, such as services.
distractorRationale.d: Wants and needs are different; needs are essential for survival, while wants are additional desires.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about scarcity is true?

options.text: Scarcity is a permanent condition in all economies.
Scarcity can be eliminated with technological advancements.
Scarcity only applies to natural resources.

questions.explanation: Scarcity is indeed a permanent condition in all economies because resources are limited, and human wants are virtually unlimited. This fundamental economic problem affects every society regardless of wealth.

distractorRationale.a: Scarcity is a universal issue and does not only affect poorer countries.
distractorRationale.c: Technological advancements can improve efficiency but cannot eliminate scarcity entirely.
distractorRationale.d: Scarcity applies to all types of resources, not just natural ones.

questions.stem: How does a scale of preference help individuals in making economic choices?

options.text: It eliminates the need for making choices.
It ranks competing wants based on their importance.
It provides a fixed amount of resources.
It ensures that all wants are satisfied.

questions.explanation: A scale of preference is a tool that helps individuals rank their competing wants in order of importance. This ranking aids in making informed choices when resources are limited.

distractorRationale.a: A scale of preference does not eliminate choices; it helps prioritize them.
distractorRationale.c: A scale of preference does not provide resources; it organizes wants.
distractorRationale.d: A scale of preference does not guarantee satisfaction of all wants due to limited resources.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a competing want?

options.text: Wanting both a new phone and a new laptop.
Wanting to travel to a nearby town.

questions.explanation: Competing wants arise when an individual desires multiple items that cannot be acquired simultaneously due to limited resources. In this case, wanting both a new phone and a new laptop exemplifies such competition.

distractorRationale.b: Eating and sleeping are not competing wants; they are both essential activities.
distractorRationale.c: Drinking water is a basic need and does not compete with another want.
distractorRationale.d: Traveling is a want, but it does not directly compete with another specific want in this context.

questions.stem: Why is it important to understand the concept of scarcity in economics?

options.text: It helps in satisfying all human wants.
It aids in making informed choices regarding resource allocation.
It allows for the creation of unlimited resources.

questions.explanation: Understanding scarcity is crucial in economics as it informs individuals and societies about the need to make informed choices regarding the allocation of limited resources to meet various wants.

distractorRationale.a: Scarcity does not allow for the satisfaction of all wants; it necessitates choice.
distractorRationale.c: Scarcity highlights the limitations of resources, not their abundance.
distractorRationale.d: Scarcity often increases competition among individuals for limited resources.

questions.stem: Which of the following best illustrates the concept of opportunity cost?

options.text: Choosing to buy a book instead of a movie ticket.
Having a job that pays ₦50,000 a month.
Receiving a gift from a friend.

questions.explanation: Opportunity cost refers to the value of the next best alternative that is foregone when a choice is made. In this case, choosing to buy a book instead of a movie ticket represents an opportunity cost.

distractorRationale.b: Having a job does not illustrate opportunity cost; it is a source of income.
distractorRationale.c: Saving money is a decision, but it does not directly illustrate opportunity cost without a specific alternative.
distractorRationale.d: Receiving a gift does not involve a choice that incurs an opportunity cost.

questions.stem: When faced with scarcity, what is the most rational action individuals should take?

options.text: Prioritize their wants based on importance.
Demand more resources from the government.
Spend all available resources at once.

questions.explanation: In the face of scarcity, individuals should prioritize their wants based on importance to make rational decisions about resource allocation. This helps ensure that the most critical needs are met first.

distractorRationale.a: Ignoring wants does not address the reality of scarcity; it only postpones decision-making.
distractorRationale.c: Demanding more resources is not a practical solution to the problem of scarcity.
distractorRationale.d: Spending all resources at once can lead to unmet needs and poor decision-making.
